newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rebels claim eastern provincial capital.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels claim eastern provincial capital.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia said on Friday it had captured the provincial capital of the pro-government province of Laghman after an overnight advance from the adjoining province of Nangarhar.

Taleban sources, quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), said Taleban militia met little resistance when they entered Mehtar Lam, the provincial capital, in the early hours of Friday as defenders had already fled.

Laghman was controlled by the party of Afghan Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who joined President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in June after a peace pact between the two former enemies. Taleban, which already controlled around half of Afghanistan, including key land routes, is seeking to topple Rabbani's government and enforce a strict Islamic order throughout the war-shattered country.

The capture of the town of Mehtar Lam, in a continuing push eastwards by Taleban, would give the rebel militia greater control over strategic eastern provinces and strengthen its challenge to the government.

Taleban sources in the main eastern town of Jalalabad, capital of Nangarhar province, told reporters on Thursday the militia forces had entered Laghman territory in a three-pronged attack, continuing an eastern sweep they began a week ago.
The other targets of the present offensive are the adjoining eastern province of Kunar bordering Pakistan and the strategic town of Sarobi east of the national capital Kabul.
Afghan sources in Pakistan say the latest Taleban advance is part of the militia's plans to capture maximum territory ahead of any internationally brokered peace deal.
United Nations Under-Secretary for Political Affairs Marrack Goulding and special peace envoy Norbert Holl arrived in Kabul on Thursday for talks with Afghan leaders.

The sources say the capture of Laghman would allow an advance on Kunar, which is ruled by a fundamentalist Islamic group called Salfis. But they said the Taleban could face resistance in the maountainous Alising and Alingar valleys north of Mahtar Lam.
Rabbani, in a speech in Kabul on Thursday, vowed to fight on and called Taleban "enemies of Afghanistan".

Reporters visiting Jalalabad saw that the city was firmly under the control of Taleban, whose militia captured it on Wednesday. Taleban fighters told citizens through loudspeakers fitted on vehicles that they had come to enforce Islam and peace.

Rabbani's government in Kabul said its forces had recaptured the strategic Hisarak district in the west of Nangarhar and part of Azra district in adjoining Logar province, cutting off Taleban's supply route from southern Afghanistan. There was no independent confirmation of this report, but AIP said government troops made some gains in Azra after heavy jet bombing.
Markets in Jalalabad were shut on Thursday after a bombing raid by a government aircraft and streets were virtually deserted.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) issued an appeal in Kabul expressing concern about the people of Jalalabad. "We would like to appeal to all sides of the war to spare the civilians," ICRC mission deputy chief Thomas Gurtner said in a statement.
